To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the NP, PB1, PB2, NS, and M genes of avian influenza viruses contribute to the attenuation of human influenza A virus in monkeys and adult humans and that the PB2 and M genes of the avian virus contribute to a new phenotype in human influenza A viruses that was not observed in the avian or human parental viruses.
the NP, M, PB1, and NS SGRs were attenuated for humans, and that the M and PB2 SGRs were also attenuated in monkeys.

the NS, M and PB2 genes of avian influenza virus are important determinants of the attenuation of ah influenza reassortants for squirrel monkeys and humans, and that a new phenotype is associated with the M and PB2 SGRs.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the genetic basis of the host range of influenza A viruses, and we have demonstrated that the avian influenza virus genes PB2 and M contribute to the restriction of replication of avian-human influenza A reassortants for humans.
the genetic determinants of influenza virus host range and pathogenicity.
the identification of genetic determinants of the attenuation phenotype of avian-human influenza A reassortants for squirrel monkeys and humans.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
avian influenza A viruses contain several genes that contribute to the attenuation phenotype and that these genes can be identified by the use of SGRs in monkeys.

the NP, PB1, and PB2 SGRs contributed to the attenuation of the 6/2 gene ah reassorant virus in monkeys and that the NS, M and PB2 S GRs contributed to the restriction of virus replication of the ah reassortant in adult humans.
the PB2 and M genes of the avian influenza virus contribute to the attenuation phenotype of ah reassortant viruses in humans.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

avian influenza A viruses have a constellation of genes that restrict replication in humans and that the avian genes that contribute to the attenuation phenotype are not the same in monkeys and humans.

the avian influenza virus NS, PB2, PB1, NP, and M genes are each required to attenuate a wild-type human influenza virus for monkeys and humans, but the PB2 and M genes may also contribute to the attenuation of a human influenza A virus in monkeys.
the PB2 and M genes are the major genetic determinants of the attenuation phenotype and that the NS and PB1 genes may contribute to the attenuation phenotype in humans.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of SGRs to identify the avian genes that contribute to the attenuation and host restriction of ah reassortants is a useful approach.
the avian influenza virus M segment is a major determinant of the attenuation phenotype.
the use of single-gene recombinant viruses can be used to identify genes that are responsible for attenuation.
